hero.headline: St. Lucie man with pancreatic cancer approved for experimental drug treatment
hero.teaser: Russell Reed, 64, spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County man battling pancreatic cancer has gained access to an experimental treatment after a two-month wait for approval. Russell Reed, 64, spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective. Reed said chemotherapy was no longer an option for him at this point in his treatment. According to his family, his oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited.

Daraxonrasib, also known as RMC-6236, is an investigational once-daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines. The drug targets mutated KRAS proteins, which drive more than 90% of pancreatic cancers. While the treatment is not yet FDA-approved, early clinical trial results have generated optimism among some patients and physicians. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope that the drug could help slow the progression of his disease. "There's a lot of anecdotal evidence and a lot of evidence from the clinical trials that show that this is the miracle drug for pancreatic cancer," Reed said. "It is not a cure, but it will give me time."

During the 62-day waiting period, Reed and his wife Marnie focused on making the most of their time together. For Marnie, the fight extended beyond just accessing the drug. "The idea of sitting here and waiting for the phone to ring is not ok with me," Marnie Reed said. She emphasized the importance of staying present during the difficult time. "You're still here, and if you don't pay attention, you're going to miss it," she said. "I don't want to miss a minute with him." The couple focused on the possibility of more family trips, more memories and more moments together.

Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed learned he had been approved to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. While daraxonrasib is not considered a cure for pancreatic cancer, the Reeds say the approval represents something they have been fighting for all along: more time together.

cards.headline: 66-year-old Fort Pierce man dead after shooting on Essex Drive in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: The St.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the victim in Tuesday afternoon's shooting on Essex Drive as Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce. Deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. to a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned an adult man had shot another adult man with a rifle.

Deputies took the suspect into custody and began providing emergency medical care to Barnes until St. Lucie County Fire District personnel arrived. Barnes was then taken to a local hospital, where he died. Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division are continuing to process evidence, conduct interviews, and work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The suspect remains in custody. Investigators say there is no threat to the public.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce rejects Little Jim's lawsuit settlement, vows to fix waterfront property management
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer from Kevin Keene, who is suing the city over its handling of the hist.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer from Kevin Keene, who is suing the city over its handling of the historic Little Jim's Bait & Tackle restaurant property. Keene told WPTV he will continue the litigation and fight. The rejection means more taxpayer dollars will likely go toward defending the case. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the settlement was not practical, particularly a provision that would have required taxpayers to vote on future waterfront land decisions. Broderick said the lawsuit does not have any merit but acknowledged controversies mentioned in it that allege a broader pattern of defective administration of city waterfront properties.

The Little Jim's case is at least the fourth waterfront property dispute WPTV has reported on and the second to result in a lawsuit. In 2023, King's Landing developer Dale Matteson threatened legal action after claiming the city sold him buildable land filled with old power plant concrete. In 2024, Fisherman's Wharf developer Chris Shelli filed suit after state records showed the city promised property it did not own. In 2025, the city abruptly canceled the Little Jim's bidding process after the land lease expired, prompting Keene's lawsuit and leaving developers Luigi and Drita Lucaj frustrated. This year, the city became responsible for nearly $200,000 in unpaid rent tied to Crabby's Waterfront Restaurant. Broderick said the city is creating a new real estate management position to track leases, rent payments, and waterfront properties with the goal of preventing these problems from happening again. Both sides say they are open to negotiating, with Keene saying he wants transparency, not money.

cards.headline: 28-year-old man dies after weekend double shooting on South 14th Street in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after he was shot multiple times in Fort Pierce early Sunday morning. A 28-year-old woman was also shot but sustained non-life-threatening injuries.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after he was shot multiple times in Fort Pierce over the weekend, according to police. The shooting happened early Sunday morning at about 3:43 a.m. in the 300 block of South 14th Street. Officers arrived at the scene and found two people with apparent gunshot wounds. The man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to a local hospital but died from his injuries on Tuesday. Officers also found a 28-year-old woman with injuries to her hand from the shooting, but her injuries were described as not life-threatening.

Police said a preliminary investigation indicated that the victims had been involved in an earlier altercation in the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As they arrived home, police said a man believed to be involved in the previous altercation approached and opened fire before fleeing the area. Police said this investigation remains active and ongoing. The names of the victims have not been released. Anyone with information in the case is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce to overhaul waterfront development process after multiple lawsuits, unpaid rent
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer from plaintiff Kevin Keene, who is suing the city over its handling of the historic restaurant Little Jim's Bait & Tackle. The rejection means more taxpayer dollars will likely go toward defending the case. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the settlement wasn't practical, particularly a provision that would have required taxpayers to vote on future waterfront land decisions. Broderick also said he feels the lawsuit doesn't have any merit, though the city has an obligation to defend it. Keene told WPTV he will continue the litigation and fight.

The Little Jim Bait & Tackle case is at least the fourth waterfront property dispute WPTV has reported on, and the second to result in a lawsuit. In 2023, the developer of King's Landing threatened legal action after claiming the city sold him buildable land filled with old power plant concrete. Developer Dale Matteson said at the time there would be litigation. In 2024, the developer of Fisherman's Wharf, Chris Shelli, filed suit against the city after state records showed the city promised property it didn't own. Shelli said the city could either pay back the money spent or end up in the courtroom. Then in 2025, Little Jim's land lease expired and the city sought bids to take over the property. Amid public outcry, the city abruptly canceled the process, prompting Keene's lawsuit and leaving at least two developers frustrated. Developers Luigi and Drita Lucaj said they were feeling quite disappointed and angry after following the city's recommendations very thoroughly. This year, the city became responsible for nearly $200,000 in unpaid rent tied to Crabby's Waterfront Restaurant.

Broderick acknowledged some of the controversies mentioned in the lawsuit, which allege a broader pattern of defective administration of city waterfront properties. When asked how the city would respond to these allegations, Broderick said he would not call it poorly managed but rather not being managed at all, an issue he takes very seriously. Broderick told WPTV the city is creating a new real estate management position to track leases, rent payments, and waterfront properties with the goal of preventing these problems from happening again. He said he will not rest until he gets to the bottom of this issue and everything is categorized and spreadsheeted.

Broderick said fixing the problem will take a top down, bottom up approach to look at the entirety of the portfolio of the city of Fort Pierce and fix this one asset at a time. Both sides say they are open to negotiating. Keene says he wants transparency, not money, and is willing to revise his offer. Broderick says he will consider any feasible settlement that keeps the case out of court.

cards.headline: Lionel Messi leads Argentina to 3-2 comeback victory over Egypt, advances to World Cup quarterfinals
cards.body:
Lionel Messi scored his eighth goal of the tournament and led Argentina to an improbable 3-2 victory over Egypt on Tuesday despite trailing by two goals with only 11 minutes of regulation time to play. The defending champions rallied from a 2-0 deficit to win their round of 16 match and advance to face either Switzerland or Colombia in the quarterfinals on Saturday in Kansas City, Missouri. Messi, who was in tears after the final whistle, scored his record-extending 21st goal at the World Cup in the 83rd minute to level the score at 2-2. Enzo Fernandez scored the winning goal in stoppage time to complete one of the great World Cup comebacks, with Cristian Romero starting the rally in the 79th minute.

Egypt had taken a surprising lead in the 15th minute when Yasser Ibrahim got ahead of Lisandro Martinez to meet Marwan Attia's cross and head the ball into the bottom corner. Argentina was quickly given the chance to level when Haissem Hassan tripped Nicolas Tagliafico in the box moments later. Referee François Letexier pointed to the penalty spot, but Egypt goalkeeper Mostafa Shobeir dove to his left to block Messi's shot for his second penalty miss of the tournament after also failing from the spot against Austria in the group stage. Messi later hit the post when the score was 1-0, and Shobeir pulled off another great save to stop Julian Alvarez from close range. Egypt thought it had doubled its lead in the second half when Mostafa Zico finished off a sweeping attack, but the wild celebrations were cut short when a foul earlier in the move was confirmed on video review and the goal was disallowed. That second goal for Egypt did come in the 67th from a similar break, and this time Zico's effort counted.

For much of the game, it looked like it would be a painful exit for the 39-year-old Messi in what might be the last of his six World Cups. Despite being the all-time leading scorer at World Cups, Messi has now missed four of eight penalty kicks at the tournament. Argentina is bidding to become the first team to win back-to-back titles since Brazil did so in 1958 and 1962.

Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni expressed his emotions after the match, saying he was so emotional and praising his group of players. Fernandez said the team never gives up and that four years have passed since Qatar, noting they have come to enjoy another World Cup and want to win it again.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach Park restroom and concession rebuild set for late 2027
hero.teaser: Beachgoers at Jensen Beach Park are waiting for the rebuild of the park's restrooms and concession building, which burned down on New Year's Eve in December 2024. The county says construction should begin in early 2027.
hero.body:
The restrooms and concession building at Jensen Beach Park remain an empty plot of land after a fire destroyed them on New Year's Eve in December 2024. Beachgoer Gonda Ghebert reached out to WPTV expressing concerns that the single small restroom facility left to serve the entire beach has become increasingly unreasonable during weekends, holidays, and peak tourist season. Frequent visitors say they also miss the cafe that previously offered convenience and amenities. "The reason I went there was because they had a nice, clean facility, showers and it was just nice coming off the deck being able to get a snack or a drink if you like," Julie Goings said. Sam Elliott added, "That's the only thing that's really missing is concessions and food availability."

Kevin Abbate, the Parks and Recreation director, explained that the permitting process takes time because of environmental considerations. "It's gotta go through the Department of Environmental Protection. We're sitting on a protected dune, so that permit is in process now," Abbate said. The design for the new 9,000 square foot Sea Turtle Beach Cafe is currently 80 percent complete. "It's about 15 feet in elevation, so there's a good seat for everyone, 100 seats and 33 at the bar," Abbate said.

The county expects final funding approval in September. Construction is planned to begin in early 2027, with a completion target of late 2027 to coincide with the winter season. The county has no plans to install additional temporary restrooms or facilities during the construction period. Abbate emphasized the importance of taking the necessary time for proper planning. "We want to do it right. If we design it properly, when we get through construction, we'll have fewer issues, it'll be a much smoother process," Abbate said.

Beachgoers who use the park regularly expressed anticipation for the new facility. "I'm hoping it moves real fast," Elliott said. Goings added, "I do want the bathrooms up and running and it would be nice to have another little convenient spot." The new Sea Turtle Beach Cafe is intended to replace the lost amenities and provide improved facilities for visitors once construction is complete.

cards.headline: Martin County School District to cut 16 administrative positions, save nearly $4 million
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District plans to eliminate 16 administrative and district-level positions, including three assistant principal positions, as part of a reorganization for the upcoming school year.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District plans to cut district staff as part of a reorganization for the upcoming school year, saving nearly $4 million from next year's budget. Superintendent Michael Maine told WPTV the plan includes eliminating 16 administrative and district-level positions, which includes three assistant principal positions and removing 42 unfilled instructional vacancies. Maine said 10 of those vacancies were held in reserve, contingent on increasing enrollment. The changes are expected to save about $3.9 million from the district's projected budget next school year. Maine said the reorganization is eliminating positions that he felt are no longer needed at the district office, so that the district takes a majority of the reduction. The Martin County School District currently enrolls 16,000 students.

Maine said the cuts reflect how the district routinely manages staffing each year based on projected student enrollment. He said the goal is to protect classroom resources while streamlining operations at the district level. Not everyone is fully on board with the scope of the cuts. Abigal, whose son will be a fourth grader at Jensen Beach Elementary this fall, said she values the small class sizes and close teacher relationships the district currently offers. She said she hopes the district is careful about how deep the cuts go.

cards.headline: Vero Beach homeowner faces $9,000 yearly insurance bill, may sell home
cards.teaser: Kelly Hagen says her homeowners insurance jumped from $6,000 to $9,000 a year, forcing her to work two jobs and consider selling her Vero Beach home.
cards.body:
Kelly Hagen reached out to share her frustration over the relentless rise in her homeowners insurance premiums. Her home, which has three bedrooms and two baths, is about 1,500 square feet and was built in 1994. Hagen said her homeowners insurance is $9,000 a year, which equates to $750 a month on top of her mortgage payment. It went from $6,000 to the next year it was $8,000. Hagen says the financial pressure goes beyond the premium itself. Her insurance company requires impact windows, an expensive upgrade she has struggled to afford while working two jobs. She works a full-time job and then works Instacart nights and weekends. Her situation was made worse when she was turned away for a $10,000 My Safe Florida Home grant after it took too long to find a contractor.

State leaders say now is the time for homeowners to shop around, pointing to new insurers entering the market with competitive rates. One new company, Stand Insurance, is offering to help homeowners connect with affordable contractors. Stand uses AI technology to study homes and then works to pair homeowners with vendors and contractors to make repairs. Dan Preston, the CEO of Stand Insurance, said if you can actually help someone be safer and have their home be safer, it's beneficial to everyone involved. Hagen said she can probably hang on just a couple more months, and then she can't do it. She will have to try and sell her house, and leaving would be devastating.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Clerk website went down for hours after third-party redirect issue
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online by 1:30 p.m.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller Michelle Miller posted a video on social media Tuesday afternoon addressing the website outage that redirected visitors to another site for hours before coming back online by about 1:30 p.m. Miller said the public should be assured that at no time was personal or confidential information compromised or at risk. She said the clerk's office does not store sensitive personal information on the public-facing website and that the website faced a temporary redirection issue caused by a third-party service provider.

Jose Clavijo, the agency's IT director, said they received a report just before 8 a.m. that something was wrong with the county clerk's homepage. Clavijo said as soon as he identified it, he told staff to turn it off and then they started the investigation. The clerk's office communications team said this wasn't a hack because there wasn't any personal information compromised. The office said residents could still access information and services on the website through direct links instead of using the homepage. Clavijo said payments, property fraud services, and all other services remained available, with only the main page affected. He said the office is working to prevent similar issues and that as soon as they identify the exact issue, there will be a tremendous remediation.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce owes nearly $16,000 in fines for unpermitted docks at Little Jim's
cards.teaser: Florida Department of Environmental Protection claims Fort Pierce has been operating docks on state-owned submerged land at Little Jim Bait & Tackle without required permits since 2021.
cards.body:
Documents WPTV obtained from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection claim the city has been operating docks on state-owned submerged land at Little Jim without the required permits since 2021. The state agency has ordered the city to pay nearly $16,000 by July 17. The FDEP action, issued in June, comes amid a lawsuit Kevin Keene filed as a local resident. Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to reject a settlement offer in the case alleging years of waterfront mismanagement tied to historic restaurant Little Jim Bait & Tackle. Under the proposed settlement terms, Keene would have dropped the case if the city halted any new plans for Little Jim until the permit issues are resolved and allowed a public vote on future waterfront land decisions.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick acknowledged the permit issue. Broderick said his information is that the accusation is actually true, that there was an extension of the existing docks. Broderick said someone at some point extended the docks further than allowed. He plans to negotiate FDEP's fines down while the city investigates who authorized the extension. Broderick said the city of Fort Pierce owns that real estate, so ultimately the city of Fort Pierce is the responsible party. Broderick also said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions to prevent future situations.

cards.headline: United States eliminated from World Cup after 4-1 loss to Belgium in round of 16
cards.teaser: Charles De Ketelaere scored twice and assisted on another goal as Belgium knocked the U.S. out of the World Cup for the second time in 12 years in a 4-1 defeat Monday night in Seattle.
cards.body:
The United States' hopes for a deep World Cup run at home ended when Charles De Ketelaere scored twice and assisted on another goal, helping Belgium expose the Americans' defensive liabilities in a 4-1 win Monday night that earned a quarterfinal berth. While the U.S. was boosted by the presence of star forward Folarin Balogun, whose one-game red-card suspension was controversially lifted by FIFA, American defenders were at fault in a pair of first-half goals and goalkeeper Matt Freese's gaffe gave the Red Devils a third early in the second half. Second-half substitute Romelu Lukaku added Belgium's final goal in the third minute of stoppage time. Seeking its first World Cup title, Belgium knocked the U.S. out in the round of 16 for the second time in 12 years and extended its unbeaten streak to 18 games. The Red Devils play 2010 champion Spain on Friday at Inglewood, California, for a semifinal berth against France or Morocco.

Malik Tillman tied the score 1-1 midway through the first half with his second free kick goal of the tournament, but the Americans conceded just 61 seconds after the ensuing kickoff. Coach Mauricio Pochettino showed his frustration by kicking a rack in front of the bench, sending four water bottles flying. American star Christian Pulisic could only watch from the bench after injuring his right foot when he hit a boot of Belgium captain Youri Tielemans on a 52nd-minute shot attempt. After winning three games in a World Cup for the first time in this expanded 48-nation tournament, the U.S. failed in its quest to reach the quarterfinals for the first time since 2002 and lost to Belgium for the seventh straight time since a victory at the initial tournament in 1930.

cards.headline: IOC ending neutral status vetting for Russian athletes ahead of 2028 LA Olympics
cards.teaser: The International Olympic Committee advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
cards.body:
The IOC advised Olympic sports bodies on Tuesday to end a three-year program vetting Russians for neutral status ahead of qualifying events for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The move was expected since the International Olympic Committee advised two months ago that athletes from Belarus, Russia's military ally in the full military invasion of Ukraine, should be allowed again to compete with their full national identity. The IOC stands in solidarity with the Olympic community of Ukraine, which the Olympic movement has supported since the beginning of the war, and will continue to do so, the Olympic body said in a statement after a meeting of its executive board.

The IOC eased entry requirements to its own events for Russian athletes and teams while provisionally lifting its suspension since October 2023 of the Russian Olympic Committee. The terms of that suspension, imposed when the Russian Olympic body incorporated regional sports councils from occupied regions of Ukraine, no longer applied, the IOC said. Just 32 athletes from Russia and Belarus competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics as approved neutrals and combined to win five medals. The Russian team had more than 300 athletes at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics and won 71 medals. The IOC did not yet approve letting Russian athletes and teams compete with their flag and anthem. That decision will come at an appropriate time, it said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Roll Past Jupiter 11-2 in Series Opener
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie Mets opened their road series against the Jupiter Hammerheads with an 11-2 rout Tuesday night at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium, leading from the first pitch to the las
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets opened their road series against the Jupiter Hammerheads with an 11-2 rout Tuesday night at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium, leading from the first pitch to the last.

Leadoff hitter Antonio Jimenez set the tone immediately, homering on the very first pitch of the game from Jupiter starter Jonas Uzcategui. Jimenez finished the night 4 for 6 with the home run, two doubles, four runs scored and two stolen bases. He came a triple short of the cycle, striking out and hitting into a fielder's choice in his final two at-bats.

Four St. Lucie pitchers held the Hammerheads to just two hits. Starter Jose Lopez, making his team debut, worked four solid innings, allowing one hit and two runs with four walks and four strikeouts. Relievers Zack Mack, Miguel Mejias and Elwis Mijares combined for five innings of one-hit relief. Mack earned the win.

The Mets built a 3-0 lead through two innings before Jupiter answered with two runs and put the tying run on third base in the fourth. Lopez escaped the jam by getting Edgardo De Leon to pop out, preserving a 3-2 lead.

St. Lucie broke the game open with four runs in the sixth. Branny De Oleo drove in a run with a single, Jimenez scored on a wild pitch, and AJ Salgado added a two-run single to push the lead to 7-2.

The Mets tacked on two unearned runs in the eighth on a Jupiter error and another run-scoring wild pitch, then closed the scoring in the ninth on a De Oleo RBI single and yet another wild pitch that brought Jimenez home.

De Oleo went 2 for 5 with three RBI and Salgado added two hits and two RBI. Julio Zayas drew four walks, while Jeremy Rodriguez walked twice and scored two runs.

The win improved St. Lucie to 8-2 at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium this season and marked its third straight victory over Jupiter. The Mets (4-10, 37-43) and Hammerheads (5-11, 42-40) continue their series Wednesday, with first pitch set for 6:30 p.m.

hero.headline: 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival Returns to Vero Beach in November
hero.body:
The 18th Annual Treasure Coast Seafood Festival will return to Vero Beach this November, according to Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. The festival is organized by the event promoter and will take place in Vero Beach.

The annual seafood festival has become a regular event for Indian River County residents and visitors to the Treasure Coast. Under The Sun Promotions, Inc. announced the return of the festival on Monday.

The festival brings seafood vendors, entertainment and activities to Vero Beach each year. The event draws attendees from across the Treasure Coast region including Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

The 18th edition of the festival will be held in November 2026. Specific dates, venue location and vendor information were not provided in the announcement from Under The Sun Promotions, Inc.

hero.headline: FDA recalls frozen Publix GreenWise organic blueberries sold across Florida after E. coli contamination
hero.teaser: The Food and Drug Administration has issued a recall for frozen Publix GreenWise Organic Blueberries due to possible E. coli contamination. The product was shipped to Publix retail stores throughout eight states, including Florida.
hero.body:
The Food and Drug Administration has issued a recall for frozen Publix GreenWise Organic Blueberries due to possible E. coli contamination. The product, sold in 10-ounce packages, was distributed to Publix retail stores throughout eight states, including Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. Customers who purchased these blueberries are asked not to consume them and should either discard them or return them to the place of purchase for a full refund.

The affected product is GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries with lot code 60401 and a best by date of February 9, 2028. The FDA has reported 12 confirmed cases of consumers experiencing stomach illness between May 11, 2026 and June 5, 2026 linked with E. coli infections. The recall comes as health officials work to prevent further illnesses associated with the contaminated product.

Those who have consumed food contaminated with E. coli can experience severe stomach cramps, diarrhea which may be bloody, and vomiting. Most healthy individuals can recover within a week. However, some infections can result in serious health complications. Consumers who have purchased the affected blueberries should check their freezers for the specific lot code and best by date to determine if their product is part of the recall.

Consumers with questions or concerns about the recall can contact Info.foodsafety@comfrut.com or call 336-899-5612. The recall serves as a reminder for shoppers to stay informed about food safety alerts and to carefully check product details when recalls are announced. Anyone who believes they may have become ill after consuming the recalled blueberries should contact their healthcare provider.

cards.headline: Leon County judge fast-tracks ballot residency challenge to GOP gubernatorial candidate James Fishback
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge has set a critical two-day hearing for July 21 and 22 to determine whether Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback meets Florida's.
cards.body:
A Leon County judge has set a critical two-day hearing for July 21 and 22 to determine whether Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback meets Florida's seven-year residency requirement to remain on the ballot. The lawsuit was filed by Lt. Jay Collins, one of Fishback's rivals in the GOP primary. Collins argues that Fishback does not meet the residency requirement, pointing to records tied to Fishback's voter registration and residency in Washington, D.C. During a Tuesday scheduling hearing, Judge David Frank warned attorneys there is an extreme shortage of time with the August 18 primary approaching. Frank noted it is likely already too late to stop ballots from being printed and explained that if Fishback is removed, there would be an injunction to the Department of State to tell the supervisors of elections not to count the votes and post a notice. Fishback's attorney, former state representative Anthony Sabatini, told the judge the case turns on more than paperwork and that Fishback's intent will be central to determining residency. Sabatini said the defense wants time to present witnesses and documents.

The courtroom fight comes just days after the issue spilled onto the debate stage during last week's GOP primary debate. Fishback, Collins and former House Speaker Paul Renner appeared together while frontrunner Byron Donalds skipped the event. Fishback pressed Collins directly over the lawsuit, getting the state's lieutenant governor to note his Florida roots before declaring case closed and demanding Collins drop the lawsuit. Fishback later accused Collins of trying to steal the election with Byron Donalds. Collins pushed back, saying the challenge belongs in court and that he respects the judicial system. For now, Fishback remains on the ballot as the case adds uncertainty to the primary calendar while election officials are already preparing ballots and candidates are running out of time to shift the race. Axios reported Tuesday that Donalds continues to tower over the field as the August 18 primary approaches through polling, fundraising and endorsements. Witness and exhibit lists are due five days before the July 21 hearing.

cards.headline: Florida households now need 17 months longer to save for home down payment than a decade ago
cards.teaser: A new study by Smart Asset found that it now takes the median-income household earner in Florida 17 months longer to save up for a down payment in 2026 than in 2016. For Floridians earning minimum wage of $14 an hour, it takes nearly 26 years to save for a down payment.
cards.body:
A new study by Smart Asset found that it now takes the median-income household earner in Florida 17 months longer to save up for a down payment in 2026 than in 2016. For Floridians who earn a minimum wage of $14 an hour, it takes nearly 26 years to save up for a down payment on a home. Florida ranked No. 25 on the list of states where saving for a down payment has become more difficult over the past decade.

Residents in Idaho have been affected the most in the last 10 years, now needing 40 months longer to buy a home than in 2016. Only three states saw median-income households able to save a down payment faster than they could in 2016: Louisiana, Mississippi and North Dakota. West Virginia has the nation's lowest down payment burden, with a median-income household needing 5.5 years to save for a down payment in 2026, just three months longer than in 2016. According to the study, saving for a down payment on a minimum-wage income alone is essentially impossible in every state.

cards.headline: Pennsylvania boy loses hand after alligator attack while fishing at Marion County fish camp
cards.teaser: An 11-year-old Pennsylvania boy named Brodie lost his dominant right hand after an alligator attack two weekends ago at Nelson's Fish Camp near Umatilla in Marion County.
cards.body:
Brodie, 11, and his father were visiting from Pennsylvania and fishing two weekends ago at Nelson's Fish Camp near Umatilla when the attack occurred. Andrew Wright, one of Brodie's relatives, said they were aware of their surroundings and had seen alligators in the area, but nothing that was close to them or of concern. The attack happened as Brodie was putting a fish back in the water that he had just reeled in. Wright said the gator came out of nowhere and they never saw it. The alligator grabbed Brodie by the arm, and his father jumped on it trying to pry its mouth open. When he did that, the gator did its roll and broke pretty much every bone in Brodie's lower arm, severing part of his hand.

At the hospital, doctors had to amputate Brodie's right hand, which Wright said is his dominant one when playing sports like baseball and football. Wright said everything that Brodie knew, doing everything with his right hand, he can't do that anymore, and physically and emotionally it's going to be a very long road for him. Despite what's ahead, Brodie remains in good spirits, as shown by his smile in photos taken after the attack. A GoFundMe for Brodie and his family had already raised more than $19,000 in donations as of Tuesday morning. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it captured and killed the nearly 9-foot alligator believed to be responsible for the attack.

hero.headline: Vision Marine Technologies plans to sell Palm City property after consolidating operations
hero.teaser: Vision Marine Technologies has completed consolidation of its tender-rigging operations at Fort Lauderdale Marina and announced a pending sale of its Palm City property.
hero.body:
Vision Marine Technologies has completed the consolidation of its tender-rigging operations at Fort Lauderdale Marina. The company announced it is planning to sell its Palm City property as part of the operational consolidation.

The company moved its tender operations from Palm City to Fort Lauderdale. The sale of the Palm City property is pending.

hero.headline: St. Lucie man with pancreatic cancer approved for experimental drug treatment
hero.teaser: Russell Reed, 64, spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County man battling pancreatic cancer has gained access to an experimental treatment after a two-month wait for approval. Russell Reed, 64, spent 62 days waiting to learn whether he would be approved to receive daraxonrasib, an experimental drug his oncologist believed could help after traditional treatments were no longer effective. Reed said chemotherapy was no longer an option for him at this point in his treatment. According to his family, his oncologist submitted a request through the FDA's Expanded Access Program, which can allow patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses to receive treatments outside of clinical trials when other options are limited.

Daraxonrasib, also known as RMC-6236, is an investigational once-daily oral pill developed by Revolution Medicines. The drug targets mutated KRAS proteins, which drive more than 90% of pancreatic cancers. While the treatment is not yet FDA-approved, early clinical trial results have generated optimism among some patients and physicians. Reed said research and clinical trial results gave him hope that the drug could help slow the progression of his disease. "There's a lot of anecdotal evidence and a lot of evidence from the clinical trials that show that this is the miracle drug for pancreatic cancer," Reed said. "It is not a cure, but it will give me time."

During the 62-day waiting period, Reed and his wife Marnie focused on making the most of their time together. For Marnie, the fight extended beyond just accessing the drug. "The idea of sitting here and waiting for the phone to ring is not ok with me," Marnie Reed said. She emphasized the importance of staying present during the difficult time. "You're still here, and if you don't pay attention, you're going to miss it," she said. "I don't want to miss a minute with him." The couple focused on the possibility of more family trips, more memories and more moments together.

Just two days after sharing their story with WPTV, Reed learned he had been approved to receive the treatment. The drug is now in his hands, and his family says he is already feeling better and optimistic about what comes next. While daraxonrasib is not considered a cure for pancreatic cancer, the Reeds say the approval represents something they have been fighting for all along: more time together.

cards.headline: 28-year-old man dies after weekend shooting on South 14th Street in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A 28-year-old man died Tuesday from multiple gunshot wounds sustained early Sunday morning in Fort Pierce. Police say the shooting followed an earlier altercation on Okeechobee Road.
cards.body:
A 28-year-old man died Tuesday after he was shot multiple times in Fort Pierce over the weekend. The shooting happened early Sunday morning at about 3:43 a.m. in the 300 block of South 14th Street. Fort Pierce police officers arrived at the scene and found two people with apparent gunshot wounds. The 28-year-old man sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to a local hospital but died from his injuries on Tuesday. Officers also found a 28-year-old woman with injuries to her hand from the shooting, but her injuries were described as not life-threatening.

A preliminary investigation indicated that the victims had been involved in an earlier altercation in the 5800 block of Okeechobee Road before returning to their residence. As they arrived home, a man believed to be involved in the previous altercation approached and opened fire before fleeing the area. The investigation remains active and ongoing. The names of the victims have not been released. Anyone with information in the case is encouraged to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Clerk's website down for hours Tuesday due to third-party service issue
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller's website was down for hours Tuesday, redirecting visitors to another site before coming back online around 1:30 p.m.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Clerk and Comptroller Michelle Miller posted a video on social media Tuesday afternoon addressing the website outage that redirected visitors to another site for hours before coming back online by about 1:30 p.m. Miller said the website faced a temporary redirection issue caused by a third-party service provider. She assured the public that at no time was personal or confidential information compromised or at risk. The clerk's office does not store sensitive personal information on the public-facing website.

Jose Clavijo, the agency's IT director, said they received a report just before 8 a.m. that something was wrong with the county clerk's homepage. Clavijo said he immediately ordered it turned off and started an investigation. The clerk's office communications team said this was not a hack because there was not any personal information compromised. Residents could still access information and services on the website through direct links instead of using the homepage. Clavijo said payments, property fraud services, and all other services remained available. The office is working to prevent similar issues from happening again. Clavijo said as soon as they identify the exact issue, there will be a tremendous remediation.

cards.headline: 66-year-old Fort Pierce man killed in Essex Drive shooting, suspect in custody
cards.teaser: Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce, died Tuesday after being shot at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive.
cards.body:
Andre Leonard Barnes, 66, of Fort Pierce, died Tuesday after being shot at a home in the 2700 block of Essex Drive. St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies responded around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned an adult man had shot another adult man with a rifle. Deputies took the suspect into custody and began providing emergency medical care to Barnes until St. Lucie County Fire District personnel arrived. Barnes was then taken to a local hospital, where he died.

Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division are continuing to process evidence, conduct interviews, and work to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. The suspect remains in custody. Investigators say there is no threat to the public.
